The words suggest that intellect in its own world is the soul’s prior mode, while the soul’s life in the natural world comes later. The author uses this to explain how the soul can be eternal in one mode and created in another.

This means that the soul is still subject to changing states; it has not reached a settled state. This is why the Qur'an commands, ‘Remain steadfast as you have been commanded.’ The reference to the body means that the body has become a place where the light of intellect reaches down through the soul. The soul joins the body's powers to the intellect, much as a link joins what begins in time to what is eternal. When bodily nature still dominates the soul, it turns its gaze outward and forgets its own reality: ‘They forgot God, so He made them forget themselves.’ This is the opposite of the saying, ‘Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.’ Scripture speaks of the record of wrongdoers in Sijjīn and the record of the righteous in ʿIlliyyīn.

As the Persian verse puts it: ‘One thing entered the earth and became earth; salt entered it and made it pure.’ When the soul ‘turns its gaze upon itself,’ it looks toward its own reality and toward the existence that makes it what it is, rather than merely toward the things it observes.

An objection may be raised. We understand why the soul's 'sin' could be called its possibility of existence. Earlier, the author explained that the descent of a soul, like the coming forth of other lower effects, depends on the limited possibilities present in its causes. But he also calls the soul's incompleteness, its being an intellect only in possibility, and its inability to receive everything at once a 'sin.' Are those not simply features of its descent from paradise? How can the descent be caused by the very thing it is supposed to explain? Moreover, these are conditions of our present world, while religious accounts and symbols place the soul's sin before entry into this world.

Two answers are possible. First, those limitations can be understood as features of the soul's forms of knowledge in the higher levels that precede material life. What appears there as a known reality becomes a natural limitation when it is expressed in material things. The natures, qualities, and acts of created beings are already present in higher forms of knowledge. Those forms are real, not mere unrealized possibilities.

Second, the limitations of souls in this life can explain their distance, on the path of return, from the intellects and beautiful forms that lie above them. There are levels of paradise associated with the divine essence, attributes, and acts, including the acts by which things are brought forth. The paradises from which Adam is said to have departed correspond to these levels, though they are not simply identical with the levels souls reach in their ascent. The descending and ascending intermediate worlds differ, as do the ways in which possibilities and impossibilities are hidden from us; yet corresponding levels in the two orders reflect one another.

The many worlds share a lasting underlying reality. What distinguishes their ways of existing is also what links them. This is especially true at the level of intellect, where division, bodily structure, size, motion, and even the distinction between one thing and another no longer apply in the ordinary way. The intellects reached by perfected souls in their ascent thus correspond deeply to the intellects through which divine generosity descends, even if they differ from one point of view.

The limitation that distances a soul from the higher paradises on its return can therefore also be called the source of its departure from the corresponding paradises in descent. We may speak of being 'sent out' or 'falling' because the soul has a natural capacity for a higher life. Most of the author's next sentences repeat this account. They make clear that the 'sin' here is natural and belongs to the order of creation, not an offence against a command. It may also be understood in a religious sense by the second reading. The words 'being an intellect in possibility' add another name for the soul's incompleteness.

An objection may be raised. If infinitely many souls existed before bodies as separate souls, they would need infinitely many bodies on which to act. That would contradict the assumption that they existed before their bodies. If they were first attached to other bodies and later entered these, the result would be the movement of souls from body to body.

But the author is not saying that countless souls already existed as separate agents acting on separate bodies. He means that their reality existed as one intelligible whole. What later acts through bodies was present there in its underlying reality, source, and perfection—not yet under the description of acting through a body. In other words, the higher intellect contains the powers and grounds of existence from which these later activities come.

The opposing philosopher may deny that souls existed before bodies as many distinct souls, without denying their prior existence as a single intelligible reality. Arguments directed against the first claim do not by themselves defeat the second.
The intellectual source has unlimited power.

A thing’s existence has three relations: to its own nature, which makes it possible; to its matter, which makes it possible to receive form; and to its cause, which gives it necessary existence. The cause gives existence and is nearer to the thing than the thing is to itself.

The confusion comes from treating existence as if it were just an idea, and from overlooking what stays the same as existence grows stronger. The cause, the receiving matter, and the connection through change let us say “it is still the same thing” without claiming an impossible change of nature.
If these three features let us say that the thing remains itself, its different natures follow from it. One reality can give rise to many ideas.
The commentator says the author’s sentence should be shortened so that it does not seem to assume what it is trying to prove.
On this view, material forms are reflections of intellectual forms, reversing the usual way of speaking. This is the meaning of the saying, “In you the greater world is folded up.”

These are thinkers who deny that one thing can have higher and lower levels while remaining one thing through change. They also deny substantial motion. Because they see only separate concepts and images, they cannot explain how we know a thing’s reality or how it exists in the mind.
The forms that exist in matter.

The soul once pointed to its body and said “I,” because it was absorbed in the body’s life. As it rises, it sees more inward levels of its own existence and can point to them as “I.” The folktale is about a man who tied a gourd to his leg so he would not lose himself in a crowd. Someone moved it to another man, and when he woke up, he pointed at the other man and said, “You are me—so who am I?”
The manuscript reads “not in possibility,” while the printed text reads “in possibility.” The manuscript reading seems more likely.

The commentator asks why the author did not interpret the philosopher’s arguments as denying the soul’s existence specifically as a soul, rather than denying its existence as an intellect. This would have avoided the objections that follow.

The commentary says all lights, whether sunlight, moonlight, lamp light, or spiritual light, belong to one kind and differ by greater or lesser strength. Just as faster and slower motion are different levels of one continuous movement, light and shadow are different levels of one kind of existence.

Souls may exist before bodies in three ways: as knowledge in the descending chain of intellects; as one intellectual reality; or through souls moving from one body to another. The first two are accepted here; the third is rejected.
“Two thousand years” is only an approximate way of speaking. The two periods may mean the intellectual and imaginal worlds, each showing a thousand divine names.

If a limited number of souls moved through an unlimited succession of bodies, they would eventually have to stop, unless new souls began to exist. That would contradict the view that souls never begin. If the number of souls were limited, they could still all have bodies at any one time, so they would not be inactive. The argument also raises other problems about many immaterial individuals of one kind.

The soul’s earlier modes may be divine, intellectual, or imaginal. They can be one and simple, with no size or direction. The imaginal world is made of forms without matter; each form there corresponds to something in this world.

The soul’s cause at the beginning need not be the same as its cause as it continues to exist. A vessel may be made by a potter but remain because its clay has hardened. Likewise, the body’s condition brings the soul into being, while the active intellect sustains it after bodily life.
A Persian poem says: “I seize existence from nonexistence; in nonexistence I am a king and a knower.” The prayer says, “O You who created things from nothing.”

“Dependence” and “action” here name actual modes of existence, not just relations between things. The author’s terms for relation, need, and dependence refer to real ways that beings exist through God.

“Soul” here means the source of perception, movement, and action in a living being. The natural form that comes before it is a lower stage in the soul’s development; the animal form that comes after it is not, by itself, a stage of the complete human soul.

An objection: if the aim is merely to show an endless chain of causes, why mention that each cause is simple? The same argument could be applied to each new event: the first needs a cause, the second needs a cause, and so on. Would there not be an infinite series even if the cause were made up of parts?

The answer is no. A cause made up of parts need not lead to that impossible infinite series. The philosopher whose proof is being examined explains the difference in his discussion of general principles. A new event requires some new condition; otherwise there would be no reason why it occurred at one time rather than earlier. If its cause is simple and must itself be new, its own cause must again be both simple and new. The same reasoning then repeats without end.

But a cause with parts might contain something eternal and a new condition. A lasting cause could produce its effect when the new condition arose or when an obstacle ceased to exist. Since the condition could even be the absence of something, this does not require infinitely many existing causes, all ordered one before another. The supposed endless chain does not follow.

Still, the original proof takes a longer route than necessary. Its author later says that the soul cannot be composed of parts. He could simply have argued: if the soul began to exist and is simple, it would need another new cause because it began and a simple cause because it is simple. Instead he first raises the choice between a simple and a composite cause. His further treatment of that choice also includes a step that is not needed for the proof.
The argument also allows the possibility that the soul and body depend on one another. Some theologians say an effect can be delayed after its cause.
A missing thing cannot have a position. A separate intellect also has no position, even though it exists.

The body may be needed only to make the soul’s relation to it possible, not to give the soul existence itself. Coming to be may mean the boundary between nonexistence and existence, not a new quality added to a thing. The body may also be a condition for the soul’s completion rather than its existence.

The condition in question is the body. It is both the condition for the soul’s beginning and the place where the soul acts, unlike the motion of a heavenly sphere, where the condition for motion is not the place where it acts.

“The soul in general” may mean the soul’s intellectual reality, or the enduring reality that remains through its stages of substantial change. It does not mean one individual soul or a general idea shared by many souls.

Some philosophers say bodily powers act only through bodily position, and therefore cannot act on their own matter. Illuminationist thinkers instead assign actions such as feeding and growth to separate forms that govern each kind.

The commentator argues that coming to be is not simply a thing’s existence; it is the boundary where nonexistence becomes existence. A condition for this boundary need not be a condition for the existence that follows it.
The cause of something beginning to exist can differ from the cause that keeps it in existence. The body may cause the soul to begin, while the active intellect sustains it.

The difficulty has two parts. First, how can an immaterial substance begin to exist only when a particular body is ready and at a particular time? Being free of matter, it should have the same relation to every time. Second, what a thing is prepared to receive ought to become one of its own states and complete it. How can a substance wholly separate from matter become a state of matter?

This is the difficult objection that the author says he will later quote from Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī in The Eastern Return. That is why he tells the reader to watch for it. The objection has force. But part of it also applies to the opposing view. Both sides must explain how a soul that eventually survives as an immaterial being can have a beginning.

One reply is that only a new relationship between body and soul begins. But on the opposing view this seems to leave the soul itself eternal: the newly arising thing is merely a relation, not the soul. That is very different from the author's account, in which the soul begins with the body and survives as spirit. At first it has a changing, bodily mode of existence. Its relation to the body is real and begins with it, but in the end the soul leaves time behind. Past, present, and future no longer apply to it in the ordinary way. Times are then present to it as though in a single moment, and places as though at a single point. Something similar is already true of its grasp of general truths, even before we consider the soul's own immaterial reality.

On the author's account the soul also passes through stages that belong to its very being. On the opposing account it has just one level, that of immaterial existence. The author will soon examine what carries the capacity for its later, enduring immaterial life. — س ره
The earlier argument was that the soul cannot be destroyed when the body dies. Here the claim is that the soul cannot perish at all.
This applies even to the agent's power to act. But an obvious difficulty arises here. Mīr Dāmād reports it from Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi in Al-Qabasāt, calling it one of the hardest problems to untangle.

If anything in the world ceases to exist, the objection goes, God's existence would also have to cease. A thing can fail to exist because one of its conditions is missing, because a condition of its cause is missing, or because part of that cause is missing. We can then ask why that condition or part is missing. The same question repeats until we reach God, since every existing thing ultimately depends on Him. Does the disappearance of a thing, then, imply a failure at the first source of everything?

The reply is that a passing event ends when its particular stretch of an ever-renewing reality ends. The author understands this as the flowing existence of material nature; other philosophers have explained it through the changing positions of the heavens. Each stage of such a changing reality is necessarily absent when a different stage is present. Friday is necessarily absent on Thursday and Saturday. No further cause is needed to explain why Friday is absent on those days.

Once the ending of an event is traced to the ending of its own stage in that flow, its absence follows from what that stage is. There is no need to explain that absence through another cause, and the chain never leads to God's being absent. The creator brings the changing reality itself into existence; He does not first create a fixed thing and then add the feature of constant passing away.
Mīr Dāmād first points toward this reply. He then offers another argument, in these terms:

“We must cut this difficulty off at its root. We have shown that coming into being and passing away in time can be understood only by tracing them to a nature whose very being is constantly renewed and spent. The continuity of that renewal and passing is what remains stable in it. It flows through successive beginnings and endings without needing an outside cause to make each stage disappear. That insight offers a way out of these difficulties. But I will now explain the matter from another direction.

“The problem becomes hard only for someone who imagines that the absence of a perishable thing is itself a new event in the world. On that view, when a thing ends, a new destruction occurs after it has existed. Its earlier existence is supposedly taken away, even from the time in which its cause brought it about. Nonexistence becomes something an agent produces, as though the agent performed an act of destroying. The thing's not being present at a later time is treated as a fact that first comes into being at that later time. And the removal of an obstacle is treated as a cause that must come before the effect it makes possible.

“None of these assumptions has a sound basis. Some who call themselves philosophers are satisfied with them, but a careful thinker knows that whatever comes into being, changes, acts, or receives an action must be something. Absolute nonexistence is not something that acts or receives action. It is pure denial: saying that a thing is not there. The word points to no new thing in reality. To say that something which exists at one time is absent later is simply to deny its presence at that later time.

“Could its existence during its own time be removed? That would amount to saying that it both existed and did not exist then. Could it be removed from a later time? That makes no sense, since it never existed at that later time in the first place.

“So passing away is properly understood as the end of the continuing gift of existence: the further sustaining of the thing is not given. The Qur'an speaks of this sustaining as preserving—‘Their preservation does not tire Him’—and as holding—‘He holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease.’ There is no absence that first comes into being. The absence of a temporal thing means that the time allotted to its existence has an ending, just as it has a beginning. Its existence, bounded at both ends, is not erased from its proper time or from the wider order in which that time has its place.

“It follows that the absence which comes after a perishable thing is not a new event needing a new cause. From the outset, the complete cause for its existing during the later time never exists. The same is true of its absence before the time when it actually begins. Neither absence is a fresh event produced when part of the complete cause of its actual existence is removed. The complete cause of an existence that really took place has not been undone. Rather, the supposed complete cause of an existence that never takes place is itself never realized.

“Our minds can imagine an endless series of such absences before and after a thing's actual life. We distinguish them by their relation to possible states of being, not because one absence physically causes another, or because the series must arrive at a last, independent absence. This should now be clear.”

That ends his illuminating account. I have quoted it at length, even though it goes beyond the usual limits of a marginal note, because it contains valuable explanations for this question and for others. The reader should think carefully about its depth and recognize the strength of the approach. — S. R.

The second argument treats perishing as a change that must have something to receive it. If the soul itself cannot be that receiver, it would need matter. But that matter would need another basis if it could perish, leading to an endless chain. The argument concludes that the final, enduring receiver is the soul itself.
The previous arguments concern a soul that exists separately from matter. They do not explain how a soul connected to the body can come into being or survive the body's loss.
The Active Intellect does not itself begin at a certain time or have a readiness to exist. It becomes the soul's storehouse of remembered ideas through a new relation to the soul.

“Receiver” can mean something ready to take on a form, or something that is acted on and completed by a form. These are different meanings. The body is a receiver of the soul in the second sense, not the first.

“Matter” can mean the source from which a thing comes, or what receives the form of the thing. The body may receive the soul-form without being the source from which the soul comes. The same difference applies to what comes to be and what can perish.
Tusi's question is whether the body can be the basis for the soul's coming into being but not for its perishing.
The author refers to an earlier answer that he had accepted and refined before he considered the question again.

The point is not that the body mistakenly demanded a power bound to matter when it actually needed a spiritual power to govern it. Natural processes do not make errors of judgment: bodily readiness does not 'choose wrongly.' Nor should we say that the Giver noticed what would suit the body and granted it a separate thinking power, for then the body would already be ready for that separate power, which is the very difficulty under discussion.

A third explanation would say that the body rightly received the bodily power it asked for, and that the Giver then added a separate spiritual reality out of sheer generosity, making the bodily power its servant or its shadow. But that would conflict with the rule that gifts are given according to readiness. If readiness were unnecessary, the same generosity could bestow a rational human soul on an ant.

The intended answer, as the author will explain, is that bodily matter is ready for a spiritual power indirectly. Divine gifts match what a thing is ready to receive, even where the readiness is of this indirect kind.

An objection follows. If the separate soul has no material subject carrying the possibility of its existence, then, by the usual rule, what has no such subject cannot begin after being absent. The soul would not come into being. If it does have a material subject, the objection seems to return. Could we say the body carries the soul's possibility only indirectly? Then it might also carry, indirectly, the possibility of the soul's passing away.

The reply accepts the force of that distinction, as the author's later account of the soul being preceded by the body's readiness suggests. But 'indirectly' must not be understood as a fiction or a merely verbal connection. Nor is this like saying that someone seated in a moving ship moves only because the ship moves. It is more like the way a natural kind exists through its particular members, or the way a general kind is present in a simple reality through what distinguishes that reality. The indirect connection is real.

The body is said to rise from the earth in the life to come because the body of that life grows out of what was formed in this earthly body and soul. Its beautiful or ugly appearance, and the forms taken by its deeds—gardens, dwellings, bitter cold, fierce heat, and other experiences—come from the person's movements, lasting habits, and character.

The forms arise through deeds and habits, as the argument that deeds take bodily form requires and as revelation describes. Yet those habits were formed through the earthly body. In another sense, the bringing forth of this body from earth is already the bringing forth of the bodies belonging to the world between death and resurrection and to the final life. Those bodies are fuller and more complete expressions of this one.

Think of a picture painted on a surface and the same picture existing without needing the surface. What makes a thing what it is lies in its form. Moreover, all three bodies have their identity through the one soul. This will be examined in the discussion of resurrection.
The author reads the quoted verse as describing stages: the body is formed, actions take shape, and the lower powers are gathered into the human being's higher life.
This note points to the three reasons given here for the soul's survival after the body's death.

A preparatory cause helps bring about an effect but does not sustain it in the way a necessary cause does. The rule about what can or cannot begin or end does not show that something cannot have a new stage of existence after an earlier one.

The qualification refers to the thing's later existence. The point is that its earlier existence, which depended on something carrying it, can be enough to make its later existence more likely even when that later existence no longer needs such a carrier.

Think of something that prepares the water of a river to flow downhill. The river's water then joins the sea. Its earlier course helped bring about its later condition, but the water no longer depends on the same setting. The first answer can also be understood in this way: this is its deeper meaning, while the earlier wording gives its outward form. There is one condition, however. In that first answer, “spiritual” must refer to the thing's continued existence, not to the way it first comes into being. Think carefully about this distinction.
The soul's separate existence follows its bodily existence as a stronger stage of the same continuing life. This is change and persistence, not a second beginning from nothing.

The body supports the soul's existence while the soul exists for and through the body. After its deep change, the soul exists in itself. The thing that holds the possibility for this change need not be the same as what holds the completed state.
The soul loses its bodily potential but continues by joining the Active Intellect. It remains through God.
The argument concerns a human soul separate from matter, not a soul-form that remains within a heavenly body.

A body's measurable size is what makes it capable of being divided in thought, and of being divided in fact. That capacity does not arise only after the body has come into existence. It belongs to what the body is, rather than being an extra condition added to its existence later.

To put it differently, the body's position, understood through its spatial relations, is part of the way it exists. It is not a later feature attached to an otherwise complete body. This establishes the point at issue.

When the author speaks of something “that has no position,” there are two reasons. First, the thing has not yet come into existence, and what does not exist has no position in relation to a body. Second, even if it were to exist, it would be free from matter; what is free from matter has no position of this kind.
“Active” can mean that something produces effects; it does not always mean that it acts with greater force.

This explanation works under the position of the philosophers who follow Aristotle. They say that the source which produces souls and brings them from possibility into actuality is the Active Intellect, identified with the tenth intellect. With God's permission, it also produces the natural world. They speak of its being entrusted with the management of the world of the elements.

But the followers of Suhrawardī, and the author himself, take a different view. They say that human souls are brought into actuality by the higher reality belonging specifically to the human kind, just as other kinds of beings have their own higher sources. It is not the higher source belonging to another species, and not simply the tenth intellect.

These philosophers accept both a series of intellects arranged above and below one another and another order of intellects standing alongside one another. But they do not limit the first series to ten, twenty, or any fixed number. They say that the higher lights descend through different levels until they reach a light too weak to give rise to any further light. This resembles visible light: each successive reflection is weaker, until no further light can be passed on. The different kinds of beings in the natural world, whether souls or bodies, depend on the parallel order, not simply on the descending series.

Moreover, in his discussion of spiritual resurrection, the author says that each kind of created thing must have a suitable link with a separate form or intellectual being. These are the angels brought near to God, called the lords of the kinds by earlier philosophers and the Platonic Forms or divine forms by those who follow Plato. That statement appears to conflict with the one made here.

Perhaps the two can be reconciled. By the Active Intellect that produces and develops souls, he might mean the higher source belonging to humankind. He could call it the source of this whole world because its visible expression contains the expressions of all the other kinds, and its higher reality brings together the powers present in their higher sources. Its relation to those sources is like the relation of its visible expression to their visible expressions.

On that reading it produces the world's forms as they contribute to the human path, not as separate kinds considered in complete isolation. The essential identities of those kinds remain. Their forms of existence differ, yet the very existence in which they differ is also what they share. All are, in this account, made from what remains of the clay of the human being. They are like mirrors reflecting that higher human reality. — S. R.

Animal-like, predatory, and demonic souls are below rational souls and cannot cause them. An angelic soul could be a cause only as actual intellect; in that role, it is not acting as a human soul but as the Active Intellect.
